newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: G20 banks to present currency clearing plans.
newsitem.headline: G20 banks to present currency clearing plans.

text.p: The Group of 20 (G20) international banks will on Tuesday outline its plans for a global clearing house that aims to reduce drastically the risks of breakdown in the $1.2 trillion daily foreign exchange market.
The plans will be presented to 2,000 bankers, broker-dealers, central bankers and exchange officials gathering in Florence for a three-day Swift International Bank Operations Seminar (SIBOS).
Swift, owned by some 3,000 banks, runs the world's largest network for transmitting payment instructions, handling an estimated $2.0 trillion of such instructions a day.
"We are making good progress and keeping to our timetable," Rob Close, G20 and payments strategy director at Barclays Bank Plc, told Reuters about the G20's plan.
A draft of the business requirements for the system has been completed and the group is on target to make a final decision on the project by year's end, he said.

The G20 was formed in 1994 by bankers, commonly called "plumbers", who specialise in large value cross-border payments. Their aim is to set up a system that would reduce risks from currency settlement.

Members include senior bankers from ABN Amro, Banque Nationale de Paris, Citibank, Credit Suisse, Deutsche Bank, Fuji Bank, HSBC Holdings, Royal Bank of Canada, Swiss Bank Corp, Societe Generale and Union Bank of Switzerland.
The G20 wants to set up a foreign exchange clearing system, based on the principle of Continuous Linked Settlements (CLS), that bridges and connects national payment systems.

Some countries, such as the U.S., Britain and Switzerland, already have national payment systems that function as Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) systems, where payments are continously calculated and settled and not just at the end of the day.
G20's system would ensure that a member bank only pays out one leg of a currency transaction if -- and only if -- they have received the corresponding amount in another currency.

At present, for example, banks in Tokyo pay out trillions of yen every day but have to wait at least one to two business days before they know definitely whether they have received the corresponding amount of dollars.

The nightmare that haunts central bankers is that the lack of such a dollar receipt -- the settlement risk -- could pose a systemic risk to the entire financial system because of the size and interdependence of settlement systems worldwide.

Turnover in the world's foreign exchange markets has soared 50 percent in the last three years to $1.2 trillion a day. But since each trade involves at least two payments, bankers estimate the actual, daily settlement flows of foreign exchange could be more than $3.0 trillion.
Although trading volume has ballooned, the settlement process has not changed substantially since the 1974 closure of private German bank I.D. Herstatt.

When Herstatt was closed by German authorities, one leg of $620 million in currency transactions had been paid into its accounts in Germany. The second leg remained unsettled in New York and Herstatt's correspondent bank refused to honour any claims.

This triggered a chain of non-payments by other parties and raised the spectre of a total payments gridlock, an event that could bring the financial system to its knees. Since that day, settlement risk has also been known as Herstatt risk.

The G20's plans have attracted considerable attention among private and central bankers following a series of reports since 1994 that have shown that many banks underestimate the size of their foreign exchange exposure and do not realise they routinely incur exposure equivalent to several days of trades.
Most recently, G10 central banks in March launched a drive to reduce settlement risk with the onus on the private banking sector to implement changes within two years.

The G10 called for immediate action by individual banks to improve their practices for measuring and managing foreign exchange exposure, improvements to national payment systems and also encouraged banking groups to develop multi-currency services that would reduce risks.
